title: Full Time Teaching Is Not Sustainable, but You Do Not Want to Quit Teaching. So, What to Do?
author: Dr Dario Emanuele
summary: Dario Emanuele names two linked problems in schools: talented teachers leaving the profession and others cutting their contracts to 0.8 or 0.6 FTE so they can use the unpaid day to catch up on planning. He cites recent workload research to argue that lesson planning and resource preparation are leading drivers of stress and attrition. His first rule of survival is to accept that the system is broken and that fixing it is not the classroom teacher's job. His central claim is that slide design is not lesson planning, because real planning is the pedagogical work of choosing questions, response mechanisms, vocabulary to model and likely misconceptions. The practical answer is to teach from pre-made decks kept close to their original state, picking one platform and spending the saved time on questioning scripts and checks. Where no deck exists, he suggests using Gemini Gems to generate a structured lesson and then reviewing only the pedagogy.
points: Emanuele separates slide production, which he calls administrative clutter, from lesson planning, which is deciding questions, response mechanisms, vocabulary and misconceptions.
Teaching from pre-made decks with minimal edits reclaims hours of planning time and moves attention to questioning scripts and diagnostic checks.
He advises choosing one resource platform and not shopping around, since comparing several sites recreates the original time sink.
Where no deck exists, AI tools such as Gemini Gems can generate a structured lesson from a prompt so the teacher's job becomes reviewing the pedagogy.
Teachers are told that systemic flaws cannot be fixed from the classroom, so the priority is protecting health, time and energy.
quotes: Essentially, educators are paying out of their own pockets to buy back the time required to do a job that should be manageable within paid hours.
Accepting this reality brings an important truth: It is not your job to fix the system.
Moving shapes around on a screen, picking color palettes, and copying-and-pasting across open browser tabs is slide production, it is administrative clutter.
When you teach 5 or 6 lessons a day, trying to combine full slide design with deep pedagogical planning is physically impossible. Something has to give, and usually, it’s your sleep.
You shift your cognitive bandwidth entirely to the decisions that actually drive learning: questioning scripts, diagnostic checks, and responsive interventions.
Do not shop around. Comparing three different websites for the “best” slide set leads right back to square one.
Teaching is an art form, but that art lies in your classroom interactions, your responsiveness, your relationships, and your clarity of instruction, not in your ability to format PowerPoint slides.
